store.0: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about basic data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's amazing to see how quickly time has passed.

store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The problems we explore in this class are fascinating, and we've been diving into dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll often write a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to at least approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas.

store.4: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second most challenging. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project where we're simulating a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about what the final product should look like. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures gracefully. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. To be honest, I've always been a gamer at heart, so this was a must-take. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.

store.8: I'm also taking an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which sounds cutting-edge, I know. Initially, it was intimidating, but the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.

store.10: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to just sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and it was fascinating to research. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.

store.12: My schedule is pretty packed, as you can imagine. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter, with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. On Thursdays, I also have Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be tough if I'm already tired from the day. Fridays are a bit more relaxed, with no scheduled classes, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or lab work. I also do some undergraduate research hours in a lab that's focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm just trying to stay on top of everything and make the most of my senior year.

store.14: The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and that's without considering any major bugs or issues with the model. The Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we also rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated. However, coordinating the schedules of five different people can be a mini-nightmare. Despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of a real job environment. I'm grateful for the opportunity to dive deep and explore these complex topics.

store.16: Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, especially if something's due the next day and I'm stuck debugging. However, it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway for me is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.

store.18: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and my schedule can get really hectic with classes and projects. My hobbies are what keep me sane, to be honest. It's funny - as intense as coding can be, I actually love everything about it. I often find that my outside interests help me come back to programming with a fresh perspective. I think it's important to take a break and not be stuck behind my laptop 24/7, even if I do enjoy tinkering with code.
store.19: Sailing is probably the first thing that comes to mind when people ask me about my hobbies. It's unique among my friends, and it's something I've been passionate about since I was younger. Growing up, my dad would take me out on these tiny sailboats near the marina. The moment I felt the rush of wind against the sails, I was hooked. Now in college, I try to keep up with sailing whenever I go back home for breaks. There's a local sailing club that rents out boats at a decent student rate, so I'll sign up for a day, invite a friend if they want to come, and spend hours on the water. I love the sense of freedom it gives me. Everything else, like looming deadlines, bug fixes in code, and group project drama, fades into the background. Out on the water, the conditions are unpredictable, and you have to stay focused. It's like solving a puzzle on a grand scale, which I think is why it appeals to my problem-solving side.
store.20: I started going to the gym regularly in college as a way to offset the effects of sitting in front of a screen all day. I used to be the scrawny kid in high school who was always hunched over a computer. A friend from the dorm taught me the fundamentals of weightlifting, including proper form for squats and deadlifts, and how to program workouts. Now, I try to hit the gym around four times a week. I'm not trying to become a bodybuilder or anything, but I love seeing incremental improvements in my strength and energy levels. If I can lift just a bit more weight this month than last, or if I have a little more energy in my daily life, I count that as a win. The gym is also a great stress-reliever after marathon coding sessions. The mental clarity I get after a good workout is unreal, and it makes me more productive and helps me sleep better, especially on those nights when I'm up late finishing an assignment.
store.21: Gaming is another hobby of mine that's closely related to my interest in technology. I'm a fan of both PC and console games, but I spend more time on PC since I'm a CS major and my computer is my best friend. Lately, I've been really into co-op survival games where you gather resources, build shelters, fend off creatures, and so on. I think this is because I enjoy problem-solving in a more relaxed environment compared to debugging a large codebase. Occasionally, I also join fast-paced shooters, especially if some friends from class are online and want to team up. It's both a social activity and a mental challenge for me. While some people view gaming as a waste of time, I believe it can be strategic and collaborative, and it's a great way to stay connected. I've also dabbled in game development, mostly experimenting with Unity or Unreal Engine for fun. I'd like to explore this further if I have the time, as bridging the gap between playing games and creating them is fascinating.
store.22: Reading has been a lifelong passion of mine, thanks to my mom's love for literature. She used to hand me fantasy and sci-fi novels when I was a kid, and I'd get lost in other worlds for hours. Even with a busy schedule now, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends. Lately, I've been obsessed with sci-fi novels that explore artificial intelligence. It's partly driven by my academic interests, as I enjoy imagining future technology and how it might blur the boundaries between humans and machines. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. These books not only provide relaxation but also help me consider the ethical and social implications of the work I'll be doing after graduation. In a way, reading is both a hobby and a means of exploring philosophical questions related to my field of study.
store.23: I know it might seem chaotic to balance all these hobbies, but I've found that scheduling them helps me maintain a healthy balance. I treat my hobbies just like I would schedule study time. For example, every Sunday, I look at my week and check the weather to see if it's suitable for a gym visit in the afternoon or a trip to the local lake to rent a dinghy. If the weather doesn't cooperate, I'll plan an indoor day with friends, either playing co-op games or working out in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to fit in – I make time for 30 minutes of reading before bed, which helps me unwind after a long day.
store.24: I also enjoy combining my hobbies. For example, I've had a day where I spent the morning sailing at the lake, then grabbed lunch, and ended the day playing video games with friends. It was interesting to discuss how the experience on the water was similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op. In both cases, everyone has a role to play – whether it's manning the sails or leading the in-game strategy. I love how each hobby, in its own way, demands teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. It's great to see how different activities can complement each other and enhance my skills.
store.25: I know it can be stressful with a packed schedule, but if you're passionate about your hobbies, you'll always find a way to make time for them, even if it's just in small increments. For example, I might not be able to read for hours on end, but I can fit in one chapter. Similarly, I might not be able to sail every weekend, but once a month works for me. And with gaming, if I have just 30 minutes to spare, that's enough to squeeze in a quick match. It's all about finding ways to make your hobbies fit into your busy lifestyle.
store.26: The best part about my hobbies is that they give me something to talk about outside of coding. I love discussing data structures and algorithms, but it's great to have other interests that showcase a different side of me. My hobby menu ranges from the calming world of reading to the thrill of sailing, from the discipline of weightlifting to the adrenaline rush of co-op games. Having these diverse interests makes life more exciting and engaging. I'm glad I could share my passion with you!
store.27: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's been really cool to be a part of that. When I was a freshman, I didn't think of research as something that would be a good fit for me. I was more interested in coding projects and hackathons, but I never considered research as an option. However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience. She told me about an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant because research seemed intimidating, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.
store.28: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience, to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In contrast to the small data projects we often work on in classes, our lab deals with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. Visualizing such large datasets to enable domain experts(like astrophysicists) to quickly extract insights is a significant challenge. One of my main tasks is to work on front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. To achieve this, I use advanced JavaScript frameworks, along with D3.js for custom visualizations. In cases where we're dealing with 3D data, I also utilize specialized libraries for volumetric rendering.
store.29: The first research project I really got involved in was about visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had these daily temperature readings from buoys all around the Pacific. The raw data was enormous, consisting of tons of files scattered across different servers, each representing a single day's worth of readings at tiny intervals. Our task was to aggregate and present the data in a coherent manner to show patterns over months or even years. I threw myself into the project: writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and designing interfaces that would allow researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. I won't lie, I was a bit freaked out when I saw my name in an official publication – it felt surreal, and it's probably one of my proudest moments in college.
store.30: These days, my research has shifted to a slightly different area, but it's still under the umbrella of data visualization. I'm currently working on immersive analytics platforms. The idea is to explore how VR or AR technologies can help scientists gain a more intuitive understanding of complex data. Think about it: looking at raw numerical data in a spreadsheet is one thing, and 2D visuals like graphs are another step up. However, being able to walk around a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment, touch it, rotate it, and highlight subsets might be a game-changer for certain fields. It's a significant leap from just coding up websites. My work involves a lot of experimentation, such as plugging in VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's all very cutting-edge, which makes it exciting. Every day, I'm forging my own path because there isn't a large, established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.
store.31: The reality of research life is quite different from what many people imagine. It's not just about coding away in a quiet corner on a mysterious project. In reality, research involves a lot of reading. Academic papers seem to never end, and when I'm trying to solve a bug with rendering volumetric data in VR, there's a good chance someone has attempted something similar and written about it in a conference proceeding or workshop. I need to comb through those papers to see if they can provide any insights. It can be overwhelming at times, but over time, you learn how to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine if a paper is relevant before diving into the details. Occasionally, when I come across something interesting, I'll share it with the rest of the lab, and we'll discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.
store.32: I also get to interact with a bunch of graduate students, both master's and PhD students. It can be intimidating at first because they're so deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it's also inspiring. There's this one PhD student in our lab who's been developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets. He's trying to integrate it with our VR platform. The idea is that when looking at a huge climate dataset, you don't need to have every single point fully loaded at once in VR—a compressed representation might be enough until you zoom in. It's a wild concept, but it's super practical for real-time performance. Working alongside him means I get to see how advanced theoretical concepts are actually applied. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room while sipping coffee and hashing out how we can offload some processing to the GPU.
store.33: We've also had the opportunity to present our research at a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus. It was a great experience. We had to distill our complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was nervous, but it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what you're doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who attended, and they shared some interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.34: As for publications, I've been fortunate enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers, and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission. The conference we're targeting is the IEEE Visualization Conference(commonly known as IEEE VIS), which is a significant event in our field. Our research focuses on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. We hypothesize that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with a plain old 2D chart. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a small set of user trials with 15 participants, recording their times and asking them to fill out a UX questionnaire. Now, we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort: I'm handling the sections on system architecture and prototype design, while someone else is writing about the user study methodology. Our principal investigator will weave everything together into a cohesive narrative. It's a balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.
store.35: Sometimes I get asked if I plan on going to grad school myself. Right now, I'm leaning towards working in the industry for a couple of years, hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building, before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. The idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge is really tempting, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts get applied in real product development. One of my mentors in the lab said that sometimes stepping into industry can give you a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, so that if you do come back for a PhD, you'll have a more practical approach.
store.36: It's not all sunshine and rainbows, though. Research can be frustrating. You might spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your entire idea has already been done—and improved upon—by a group in Europe or somewhere else. That can be a tough pill to swallow. However, the key is to adapt. We'll read that existing paper, incorporate their findings, think of a new angle or a new application, and push the boundary. That's the essence of research. You're never truly starting from scratch; you're building on this giant foundation of what others have done. The sense of collaboration—both within our lab and among the global research community—is something I find really special.
store.37: One story that really stands out was when one of our massive servers crashed a few months ago. We had vital data stored there, some of which wasn't fully backed up(I know, rookie mistake, but we learned from it). I remember the scramble that night: a frantic email chain, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to see if we could recover the data. We did manage to restore most of it, but that crisis hammered home the importance of data backups. After that fiasco, we set up a better backup system and implemented some checks to ensure we never again rely on a single point of failure. It was stressful, but also kind of a bonding experience for the whole lab.
store.38: Another big plus of research is that it connects me with professors on a more personal level than just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is super approachable; if I have a question about the direction of my career or something I'm struggling with in class, I know I can pop into her office and chat. She's been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I even got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics that was filled with academic experts from all around the world. Witnessing them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even gently tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
store.39: That's basically my journey in the research world so far. It's a lot of work, often more chaotic than you'd expect, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might end up shaping the way scientists understand their data five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive stuff we're trying to pioneer will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'Hey, I was part of that from the beginning.' It's that sense of contributing to something bigger that really keeps me motivated. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, I know this experience has changed how I think about computer science, about innovation, and even about teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergrad years without it—it's definitely enriched my whole perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
